It saw a renewed rise in popularity between 1933 and 1941,but remained below the levels of the turn of the century. Since the end of the 1940s,it became very rare; when used at all it was generally as a middle name. Altweibersommer*!0At least in the meaning "Indian summer",seemingly from alt,literally "old women's summer". Compare from Hungarian vénasszonyok nyara,from Polish babie lato,archaic from Czech babské léto,from Russian ба́бье ле́то,from Belarusian ба́біна ле́та,from Ukrainian ба́бине лі́то,and from English old wives' summer; compare also from German litgirls' summer; the Polish and Czech terms for the season are also used for the webs. DWDS suggests the use for cobwebs could be comparing them to old women's white hair,like the name of the wood anemone,@-6gras,and a regional name for cottongrass,alte Mägde.<ref name"DWDS">{{R:DWDS</ref> Alternatively,the middle element Weib may be a regional variant of Spinnwebe (cognate to from English web),or related to weben (meaning,and related to,from English weave).}Compare from English gossamer,traditionally taken to be from "goose summer" and to have originally referred to the season (like from Scots St Martin's summer) and then to webs;<ref name"MWWH">''The Merriam-Webster New Book of Word Histories'' (1991),page 202,"gossamer"</ref> DWDS considers the connection of that word with ''summer'' and this word with Sommer uncertain, but besides other summery words for the webs like Sommerfäden (cognate to from Dutch litsummer-threads),fliegender Sommer,and Mariensommer,there are words like Herbstfäden.é0/altˈvaɪ̯bɐˌzɔmɐ/}Ⓓ6/63/De-@^.ogg}Alt+wei+ber+som+mer|Noun}(mask.)}#loose gossamer or cobwebs found in the air or on the ground}#Indian summer (a stretch of warm days in autumn)|Synonyms}Nachsommer,Mädchensommer

anderthalb*!H andar halb,`b litsecond half. ''Anderthalb'' is the single surviving relic of an older system to describe fractions,which counted from the higher ordinal number rather than the lower cardinal. Compare from Old English ōþer healf,from Dutch @-5half,from Danish halvanden. Compare also the use of the word halb in the sense of a half-hour before the following hour,such as ''halb zwei'' to mean one thirty. The word @-5er has since lost the meaning "second",being used solely as "other" in modern German.é0/andərthalb/,ˈɑndɐtʰˈhɑlpʰ,ˈandɐtʰˈhalpʰ,(most of Germany) some of Austria}/andərthalb/,ˈɑnd̥ərtˈhɑlb̥,(Switzerland) some of Austria and southern Germany}Ⓓ6/64/De-@^.ogg|Numeral}#one and a half (1½),sesqui-}•synononym:eineinhalb}•In den vergangenen '''@^''' Jahren haben wir also schon einiges erreicht.}•In the last '''one-and-a-half''' years,we have notched up some achievements.
